Chapter 7: The Evolution of Complex Organs and Irreducible Complexity
You’ve probably heard the argument that some parts of life are just too complicated to have evolved—they’re called “irreducibly complex.” The idea is, if you take away even a single piece, the system stops working, so it couldn’t have come together bit by bit. Think about things like the bacterial flagellum, or the blood-clotting system. Some folks claim these structures must have been designed all at once.
But here’s the thing—evolution isn’t just about building something from scratch. It’s more like tinkering with what’s already there. Nature loves to repurpose and modify existing parts, often in surprising ways.
There’s a great example involving the bones in our ears. Did you know that, way back in our reptile ancestors, these bones were actually part of the jaw? Over millions of years, they shifted roles and became crucial for hearing in mammals. That’s called co-option—where a structure that evolved for one purpose gets adapted for something completely new.
Another concept that really helps explain this is “scaffolding.” Imagine putting up a building. You use temporary supports to help it rise, but once it’s finished, you take the scaffolding down. Evolution works a lot like that. Some features develop with the help of temporary stages—intermediate forms—that later disappear or get transformed. What looks “irreducibly complex” now might have had a whole series of useful, workable steps along the way.
So, how do complex systems actually evolve? Here are a few key ideas to keep in mind:
First, evolution modifies and combines simpler parts to make something new. Second, structures aren’t stuck with just one job—they often serve multiple functions over time, which opens up room for gradual changes. And third, those temporary “scaffolding” stages can support the journey toward brand-new features.
There’s no shortage of real-world examples. Take the evolution of the eye, the immune system, or the amazing machinery inside every cell. Each one shows how complexity can build up, step by step. As long as each new stage offers some advantage, it sticks around—and, over time, those steps add up to systems that might look impossibly complex when we look back.
So, the next time you hear someone say a feature is “irreducibly complex,” just remember: what seems impossible in hindsight often makes perfect sense when you follow the path evolution took, one small step at a time.
